title: How to Start a Career in Real Estate Before Graduation - University of New Hampshire
content: Amanda Clifford ’26 works at her desk at the Residences on Madison in Worcester, Mass. Are you interested in a career in real estate but unsure which path might be right for you? Recent UNH Paul College alum Amanda Clifford made her way into the profession by focusing on entrepreneurial studies and pairing it with the real estate finance and investments minor. During her final semester, Clifford interned with CP Management. When the company learned she would be moving back home to Shrewsbury, Mass., after graduation, an opportunity emerged at a nearby property. Before graduating, Clifford had accepted a full-time position as leasing manager at the Residences on Madison, a new property managed by CP Management in Worcester. “Entrepreneurial studies complemented the real estate finance and investments minor because it taught me to look at real estate from more than just one perspective. The minor gave me more of the technical and industry-specific knowledge, while my major taught me how to recognize opportunities, think creatively, solve problems, and understand what goes into running and growing a business,” Clifford says. "I think that combination has shaped how I look at my career. Rather than feeling like I have to follow one specific path within real estate, I’m interested in gaining experience in different areas of the industry and eventually using what I learn to create opportunities for myself.” Clifford discusses how her UNH experience and internship helped launch her career in real estate and shape where she hopes to take it next. I helped the company internally by updating files in its shared drive, developing marketing ideas for specific properties, and conducting market research. I also worked on-site at one of the properties the company managed. There, I mainly helped with administrative tasks, but I was able to watch the leasing process from start to finish, which was helpful when I started my current job. I was able to watch real estate professionals do their jobs and see how they interact and what goes into being a property manager. I learned how to communicate with residents, vendors, and coworkers, how to handle problems as they come up, and how much goes into keeping a property running day to day. I also had the opportunity to attend networking events and see a different side of the industry. My job is to bring in prospective residents, give tours, review applications, and get leases signed. I also run the company's social media accounts. Once someone moves in and becomes a resident, they work with the property manager. Anything before that is my responsibility. Taking the Real Estate Finance course was beneficial. I learned a lot about how the real estate industry works, including how to conduct market research and property analyses and build pro formas. Taking classes before starting my internship helped me understand that real estate is about much more than buying and selling houses. Watching property managers in action and attending networking events during my internship showed me how many facets there are to the industry and how many different career opportunities there are to explore. I've always been interested in real estate because of the freedom and flexibility it can provide, both financially and in terms of different career paths. I've always seen myself working in real estate, whether full time, on the side, or something I pick up later in life. When I saw the new minor, I realized I had already taken many of the required courses and knew it would be beneficial to me in some capacity. The experience helped me narrow down my future plans and goals in ways I didn't realize I needed. I genuinely don't know where I'd be right now had I not pursued the minor and internship. I certainly wouldn't have as clear an idea of where I want to take the next five years or where I want to be in my career. I had no idea it would help provide me with the opportunity to have a full-time job lined up before graduating! I don’t necessarily have one specific position or path that I’m set on, and I think that’s partly because there are so many different directions I could take within real estate. My biggest goal is to keep gaining experience, learn as much as I can, and become financially stable enough to have more freedom in the choices I make. I also hope to have started taking steps toward working for myself in some capacity, whether that’s through real estate, entrepreneurship, or a combination of the two. I know ultimately, I want to build a business of my own. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Syracuse 66-3 New Hampshire (6 Sep, 2026) Game Recap - espn.com.au
content: SYRACUSE, N.Y. -- — Steve Angeli passed for three touchdowns in his first game action following a season-ending injury nearly a year ago, freshman Shavane Anderson ran for three more, and Syracuse routed New Hampshire 66-3 Saturday in the Orange’s season opener. Angeli, who suffered a torn Achilles in Syracuse’s fourth game last season, was sharp in his return. He completed 20 of 29 passes for 263 yards and touchdown strikes of 19 and 18 yards to Umari Hatcher and 27 yards to David Clement. “I think it was solid. I think there's some things we left out there,” Angeli said. “Really happy for some guys getting involved and, you know, putting up the points we did, but I think there's a lot left out there that we're going to clean up this weekend and the next week.” The quarterback threw a scare into the Orange faithful when he appeared to injure his right knee midway through the second quarter, but he ran off the field and missed just one play. “Just got a little banged up. All good. There's no injury,” said Angeli, who left the field in a foot race with coach Fran Brown. “I started talking to God before I went to him,” Brown said. “As he moved his leg and got up to walk I was like, 'race me.' He's a competitor, That's why I ended up doing that. Once he was able to do that I was very thankful." Despite the scare and Syracuse up by an insurmountable margin, Angeli played until 10 minutes were left in the game. “Our team’s a young football team,” said Brown, who graded Angeli a 75 for the afternoon. “Steve started I think five games, maybe, before this game so he hasn’t had a lot of reps, and hasn’t been able to play with the line. They don’t have much experience. The best way to get better is to continue to play." Syracuse came out sluggish but then scored on six consecutive drives. The Orange amassed 513 yards of total offense to 155 for New Hampshire (0-2). Anderson ran for 102 yards in his Syracuse debut. Tylik Hill ran for 90 more and a 2-yard score. Ten Syracuse players caught passes, led by Hatcher who had eight for 147 yards. New Hampshire's Brooks Bentley played just the first half and finished 11-of-18 passing for 75 yards and one interception. The Syracuse defense shut down the ground game, holding the Wildcats to 51 yards, and just 99 through the air. Running back Myles Thomason had seven receptions for 53 yards out of the backfield. “A tough, tough day today,” New Hampshire coach Sean Goldrich said. “We got to be better just overall at the quarterback spot and be able to run the ball. I mean, we netted no yards today and the run game, I mean, the focus all week was be able to establish the run. If you can't do that, then you put too much pressure on your system.” Syracuse was penalized 12 times for 130 yards, but Brown didn't seem overly concerned, saying they happened due to aggressiveness, not laziness. New Hampshire: Things looked encouraging after the Wildcats forced the Orange to punt on Syracuse’s opening series but then it was all downhill from there. New Hampshire, quite simply, was overmatched on both sides of the ball. Syracuse: The big story was how Angeli would fare after his injury and whether he’d come out of the game with no ill effects. He answered those questions resoundingly with his passing and his ability to withstand some big hits. The challenge increases next week. New Hampshire: Home against Stonehill Sept. 12.
